people.name: Juba II
people.fullName: Gaius Julius Juba, King of Mauretania
people.summary: Son of the Numidian king Juba I, paraded as a child in Caesar's triumph of 46 BC and raised in Rome, Juba was made king of Mauretania in 25 BC and married Cleopatra Selene; a learned Greek author, he ruled from Iol Caesarea for nearly fifty years.
people.detail: He wrote in Greek on Libya, Arabia (for Gaius Caesar's eastern expedition), Roman antiquities, the theatre and painting, works much cited by Pliny the Elder. He sent expeditions to the Canary Islands (the Fortunate Isles) and to the Purple Islands off Mogador, and named the euphorbia plant after his physician Euphorbus. His coins carry Latin legends for himself and Greek for his queen. He served in the Cantabrian war and on Gaius's eastern staff.

people.name: Cleopatra Selene
people.fullName: Cleopatra Selene II, Queen of Mauretania
people.summary: Daughter of Mark Antony and Cleopatra VII, twin of Alexander Helios, Cleopatra Selene walked in Octavian's triumph of 29 BC, was raised by Octavia and married to Juba II, ruling Mauretania with him and promoting Ptolemaic and Egyptian imagery at Caesarea.
people.detail: Her coins bear Greek legends (BASILISSA KLEOPATRA) with crocodile and Isis symbols, asserting her Ptolemaic descent. Her death is placed c. 5 BC, linked by some to an epigram of Crinagoras on a lunar eclipse. Her son Ptolemy succeeded Juba.

people.name: Livy
people.summary: Historian from Patavium whose 142-book history of Rome from the foundation to 9 BC, written over some forty years under Augustus, became the canonical narrative of the Republic; 35 books survive.
people.detail: Livy held no public office and seems to have lived at Rome on private means, on friendly terms with Augustus, who called him a Pompeian, and encouraging the young Claudius to write history. Asinius Pollio sneered at his "Patavinity". A man from Gades travelled to Rome only to see him (Pliny, Letters 2.3). He returned to Patavium and died there in AD 17.

people.name: Vitruvius
people.summary: Architect and military engineer who served Caesar and Octavian on artillery and dedicated to Augustus the ten books On Architecture, the only complete architectural treatise from antiquity.
people.detail: He built the basilica at Fanum Fortunae and received a pension through Octavia. His treatise covers urban planning, materials, temple design, acoustics of theatres, aqueducts, sundials and machines. Rediscovered at St Gall in 1416, it shaped Renaissance architecture from Alberti to Palladio.

people.name: Strabo
people.summary: Greek geographer and historian from Amaseia in Pontus whose seventeen-book Geography, completed under Tiberius, is the fullest description of the Augustan world.
people.detail: From a family that had served Mithridates VI and then gone over to Lucullus, Strabo studied at Nysa and Rome, travelled with Aelius Gallus in Egypt (25-24 BC) and wrote a lost history continuing Polybius. He was a Stoic and admirer of Augustan peace.

people.name: Nicolaus of Damascus
people.summary: Peripatetic philosopher and historian, adviser and envoy of Herod the Great, author of a 144-book Universal History and a Life of Augustus, both partly preserved, which are major sources for Josephus.
people.detail: He tutored the children of Antony and Cleopatra, then served Herod, defending the Jews of Ionia before Agrippa (14 BC), reconciling Herod with Augustus (8-7 BC) and pleading for Archelaus at Rome in 4 BC. His Life of Augustus is the earliest biography of the princeps, covering his youth and Caesar's assassination in vivid detail.

people.name: Antonius Musa
people.summary: Greek freedman physician of Augustus who cured the princeps of his near-fatal illness in 23 BC with cold baths and cold drinks, and was rewarded with a statue and equestrian rank; the same treatment failed to save Marcellus.
people.detail: Horace (Epistles 1.15) took a cold-water cure on his advice. His brother Euphorbus was physician to Juba II. Several pharmacological works were attributed to him later.

people.name: Vipsania Agrippina
people.summary: Daughter of Agrippa by his first wife, Caecilia Attica, granddaughter of Cicero's friend Atticus; first wife of Tiberius and mother of Drusus the Younger, she was divorced in 11 BC on Augustus's orders so that Tiberius could marry Julia.
people.detail: She then married Gaius Asinius Gallus, bearing him at least five sons. Tacitus says she alone of Agrippa's children died naturally, in AD 20. Tiberius never forgave Gallus for marrying her.

people.name: Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus
people.summary: Consul in 16 BC, husband of Antonia the Elder (Antony and Octavia's daughter) and grandfather of Nero, Ahenobarbus crossed the Elbe as legate in Germany, set up an altar to Augustus beyond it and built the causeways called pontes longi.
people.detail: Suetonius describes him as arrogant, extravagant and cruel, a keen charioteer who staged gladiatorial shows so bloody that Augustus had to restrain him. Augustus named him in his will. His son Gnaeus married Agrippina the Younger and fathered Nero.

people.name: Cossus Cornelius Lentulus
people.summary: Consul in 1 BC who as proconsul of Africa (c. AD 6) defeated the Gaetuli and Musulamii, winning triumphal ornaments and the cognomen Gaetulicus for his son; late in life he was Tiberius's trusted urban prefect, reputedly a heavy drinker who never betrayed a secret.
people.detail: Seneca (Epistles 83.15) records that Cossus came drunk to the Senate and had to be carried home, yet Tiberius confided matters to him that he would tell no one else. His son Cn. Lentulus Gaetulicus commanded Upper Germany for ten years until Caligula executed him in 39.

people.name: Lucius Calpurnius Piso the Pontifex
people.summary: Son of Caesar's father-in-law, consul in 15 BC, Piso crushed the Bessian revolt in Thrace (13-11 BC) and served as urban prefect for some twenty years under Augustus and Tiberius; Horace addressed the Ars Poetica to him and his sons.
people.detail: Velleius praises his combination of vigilance and apparent indolence. Like Cossus he was said to have earned Tiberius's confidence during long drinking sessions. Tacitus records his state funeral in 32.

people.name: Labeo
people.summary: Leading jurist of the Augustan age and founder of the school later called Proculian, Labeo, a republican by conviction, refused the consulship Augustus offered and wrote some 400 books, of which fragments survive in the Digest.
people.detail: His father was among Caesar's assassins and died at Philippi. He divided his year between teaching in Rome and writing in the country. Innovative in method, he drew on grammar and dialectic. Gellius and Pomponius record his frank opposition to Augustus, who mocked him in the Senate.

people.name: Ateius Capito
people.summary: Jurist and consul suffect in AD 5, a loyal servant of Augustus and Tiberius, Capito founded the school later called Sabinian and served as water commissioner from 13 to his death.
people.detail: Tacitus contrasts him with the independent Labeo: Capito's obsequiousness was rewarded with a consulship. In 15 he chaired the commission on the Tiber floods. He wrote on pontifical law and on the duties of senators; Suetonius records him flattering Tiberius that he could grant citizenship to words.

people.name: Masurius Sabinus
people.summary: Jurist of modest means who under Tiberius became the first equestrian granted the right to give opinions by the emperor's authority; his three books on civil law (Libri tres iuris civilis) became the standard framework for later commentaries "ad Sabinum".
people.detail: He lived on fees from his pupils and reached the equestrian order only around fifty. The Sabinian school took its name from him. Ulpian, Paul and Pomponius wrote huge commentaries following his order.

people.name: Judas the Galilean
people.summary: Leader of the resistance to the census of Quirinius in AD 6 who taught that paying tribute to Rome was slavery and that God alone was master; Josephus calls his movement the "fourth philosophy" and traces the later revolt to it.
people.detail: His sons James and Simon were crucified c. 46-48; Menahem, son or grandson, led a faction in 66; Eleazar ben Yair, commander at Masada, was a descendant. Acts 5.37 says he perished and his followers were scattered.

people.name: Herod Antipas
people.fullName: Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea
people.summary: Son of Herod the Great and Malthace, tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea from 4 BC to AD 39, builder of Sepphoris and Tiberias, who executed John the Baptist and, in Luke's account, examined Jesus; Caligula exiled him to Gaul in 39.
people.detail: His divorce of Aretas IV's daughter to marry his niece Herodias led to war with Nabataea and a disastrous defeat c. 36. Jesus called him "that fox" (Luke 13.32). He enjoyed Tiberius's favour and hosted the meeting of Vitellius and Artabanus.

people.name: Herodias
people.summary: Granddaughter of Herod the Great and Mariamme, sister of Agrippa I, Herodias left her husband (another Herod) to marry his half-brother Herod Antipas; the gospels blame her for the execution of John the Baptist.
people.detail: Her daughter by her first marriage is the Salome of later tradition, named by Josephus. Ambitious for royal title, she pushed Antipas to seek it from Caligula, which led to his exile; she chose to share it.

people.name: John the Baptist
people.summary: Jewish ascetic prophet who preached repentance and baptism in the Jordan in the late 20s, baptised Jesus, and was executed by Herod Antipas at Machaerus; Josephus and the gospels both record him.
people.detail: Luke makes him a kinsman of Jesus born to the priest Zechariah. His movement survived his death, with disciples at Ephesus in the 50s and the later Mandaeans claiming descent from it.

people.name: Caiaphas
people.summary: High Priest of the Jerusalem Temple from c. 18 to 36, the longest tenure of the Roman period, son-in-law of the former High Priest Annas, who according to the gospels presided over the hearing that handed Jesus to Pilate.
people.detail: His long tenure suggests close cooperation with Pilate; both were removed by Lucius Vitellius in 36-37. An ossuary inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas" found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1990 may be his.

people.name: James the Just
people.summary: Brother of Jesus, leader of the Jerusalem church from the 40s, known for strict Torah observance; Paul met him in Jerusalem and he presided at the apostolic council. The High Priest Ananus had him stoned in 62.
people.detail: Paul lists him as a witness of the risen Jesus (1 Corinthians 15.7). Josephus records his execution. The epistle of James is attributed to him. Later tradition, through Hegesippus, made him a Nazirite who prayed in the Temple until his knees were like a camel's.

people.name: Stephen
people.summary: Leader of the Greek-speaking followers of Jesus in Jerusalem, one of the seven deacons of Acts, stoned c. 34 after a speech against the Temple; venerated as the first Christian martyr.
people.detail: His relics were "discovered" at Kfar Gamla in 415, an event that spread his cult across the Mediterranean, including to Augustine's Hippo.

people.name: Barnabas
people.summary: A Cypriot Levite in the Jerusalem community who introduced Paul to the apostles, led the church at Antioch and accompanied Paul on the mission to Cyprus and Galatia, before they parted over John Mark.
people.detail: He sided with Peter at the Antioch incident (Galatians 2.13). The Epistle of Barnabas (c. 130) is wrongly attributed to him. The church of Cyprus claims him as founder.
people.death: unknown; later tradition says martyred at Salamis

people.name: Aretas IV
people.fullName: Aretas IV Philopatris, King of the Nabataeans
people.summary: King of the Nabataeans from 9 BC to AD 40, under whom Petra reached its height (the Khazneh is often attributed to his reign); he defeated Herod Antipas c. 36 and controlled Damascus when Paul escaped it.
people.detail: Augustus was angry that he took the throne without permission but recognised him. His daughter's divorce by Antipas caused the war. His coins call him "lover of his people". His reign is the most prolifically attested in Nabataean inscriptions.

people.name: Artabanus II
people.summary: Arsacid king of Parthia c. 12-38, of partly Dahae descent, who displaced the Roman-raised Vonones, sought to put his sons on the Armenian throne and clashed with Tiberius's diplomacy, before reaching terms with Lucius Vitellius on the Euphrates.
people.detail: Tacitus says he wrote to Tiberius demanding Augustus's treasure and threatening to reclaim the lands of Cyrus and Alexander. He was briefly driven out by Tiridates III in 36 but returned. His sons Vardanes and Gotarzes fought for the succession.

people.name: Pharasmanes I
people.summary: King of Caucasian Iberia who, as Tiberius's ally, installed his brother Mithridates in Armenia in 35, defeating the Parthians with Alan help; later he encouraged his son Radamistus to murder Mithridates and seize Armenia (51).
people.detail: Tacitus portrays him as ambitious and ruthless; he eventually executed Radamistus for treason to win Roman favour (58). The Harmozica inscription of 75 shows Roman support for his successor Mithridates.

people.name: Mithridates of Armenia
people.summary: Iberian prince installed as king of Armenia by Tiberius in 35, recalled and imprisoned by Caligula, restored by Claudius in 42, and murdered by his nephew Radamistus at Gorneae in 51.
people.detail: His fate exposed the weakness of the Roman garrison commanders in Armenia and opened the way for the Parthian candidate Tiridates.

people.name: Radamistus
people.summary: Son of Pharasmanes I of Iberia who seized Armenia in 51 by murdering his uncle Mithridates after a false oath, was expelled by the Parthian Tiridates, and was executed by his own father c. 58.
people.detail: His flight from Armenia with his pregnant wife Zenobia, whom he stabbed and threw into the Araxes rather than leave her to the enemy, became a famous scene (and the subject of Handel's opera Radamisto, 1720).

people.name: Lucius Vitellius
people.summary: Father of the emperor Vitellius, a skilful governor of Syria (35-39) who outmanoeuvred Parthia, removed Pilate and Caiaphas, and later became Claudius's indispensable colleague, three times consul and censor in 47-48.
people.detail: Tacitus and Suetonius present him as a model of courtly flattery: he worshipped Caligula as a god, carried Messalina's slipper inside his toga and kissed it, and urged the Senate to approve Claudius's marriage to his niece Agrippina. Yet his eastern governorship was capable and humane toward the Jews.

people.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
people.summary: Consul in AD 8 who as proconsul of Africa won the first Roman victory over Tacfarinas in 17, gaining triumphal ornaments; Tacitus notes that the glory returned to the house of the great Camillus after four centuries.
people.detail: His son Furius Camillus Scribonianus led the failed revolt in Dalmatia against Claudius in 42. His daughter Livia Medullina was engaged to the young Claudius but died on the wedding day.

people.name: Vannius
people.summary: Quadian noble whom Drusus the Younger made king over the followers of Maroboduus and Catualda settled beyond the Danube in 19; he grew rich on raiding and trade for thirty years until his nephews Vangio and Sido, backed by the Hermunduri and Lugii, overthrew him c. 50.
people.detail: Claudius refused to intervene militarily but gave him refuge in Pannonia. The kingdom lay between the rivers Marus (Morava) and Cusus.

people.name: Rhescuporis II
people.summary: Brother of Rhoemetalces I who received the wilder western part of Thrace on his death (AD 12), murdered his nephew Cotys at a banquet in 19, and was tried at Rome, exiled to Alexandria and killed there.
people.detail: His son Rhoemetalces II kept the western kingdom after his fall.

people.name: Artaxias III
people.summary: Son of Polemon I of Pontus and Pythodoris, crowned king of Armenia by Germanicus at Artaxata in 18 under the name Artaxias; his long peaceful reign ended with his death c. 34.
people.detail: A rare Roman coin of Germanicus shows him crowning Artaxias with the legend ARTAXIAS GERMANICVS.

people.name: Polemon II
people.fullName: Marcus Antonius Polemon, King of Pontus
people.summary: Son of Antonia Tryphaena, raised with Caligula, who gave him Pontus in 38; Claudius added part of Cilicia. Nero annexed Pontus in 64. He married Agrippa II's sister Berenice, who soon left him.
people.detail: His coins carry his own and the emperors' portraits; for Berenice he underwent circumcision.

people.name: Asinius Gallus
people.summary: Son of the historian Asinius Pollio, consul in 8 BC, who married Tiberius's divorced wife Vipsania and spoke with provocative freedom in the Senate; arrested in 30, he died of starvation in custody in 33.
people.detail: Augustus reputedly named him among men "eager but unequal" to the principate. He wrote a comparison of his father and Cicero, to which Claudius replied. Five of his sons reached the consulship.

people.name: Valerius Maximus
people.summary: Author of the nine books of Memorable Deeds and Sayings, a collection of moral exempla dedicated to Tiberius c. 31, who had accompanied his patron Sextus Pompeius (cos. AD 14) to Asia.
people.detail: His work, despised for its rhetoric, was enormously read in late antiquity and the Middle Ages.

people.name: Apion

roles.t: Grammarian; envoy of the Alexandrian Greeks

people.summary: Alexandrian Homeric scholar and showman lecturer who led the Greek embassy against the Jews before Caligula in 39-40; his anti-Jewish writings provoked Josephus's Against Apion.
people.detail: He lectured in Rome under Tiberius and Claudius; Tiberius called him "the cymbal of the world". Aulus Gellius preserves his story of Androcles and the lion, which he claimed to have witnessed in the Circus Maximus.

people.name: Julia Livilla
people.summary: Youngest child of Germanicus and Agrippina the Elder, exiled by her brother Caligula in 39 for her part in the Lepidus plot, recalled by Claudius in 41, then exiled again on Messalina's charge of adultery with Seneca and starved to death.
people.detail: Her fall and Seneca's exile illustrate the struggle for influence at Claudius's court.

people.name: Pallas
people.summary: Greek freedman of Antonia Minor who as Claudius's financial secretary amassed a fortune of 300 million sesterces, promoted Agrippina's marriage and Nero's adoption, and was dismissed by Nero in 55 and killed in 62.
people.detail: His brother Antonius Felix was procurator of Judaea. The Senate's honours for him in 52 were Pliny's symbol of the shame of the Claudian court.

people.name: Aulus Didius Gallus
people.summary: Senator who installed Cotys I in the Bosporan kingdom c. 45 and as governor of Britain (52-57) held the line against the Silures and intervened in the Brigantian civil war, though Tacitus calls him elderly and content to let others act.
people.detail: An inscription from Olympia lists his long career, including curator aquarum and proconsul of Asia.

people.name: Mithridates of the Bosporus
people.fullName: Tiberius Claudius Mithridates, King of the Bosporus
people.summary: King of the Cimmerian Bosporus installed by Caligula, deposed by Claudius in favour of his brother Cotys I, he tried to regain the throne with Sarmatian allies, surrendered in 49 and lived in Rome until Galba executed him.
people.detail: His defiant words to Claudius impressed the emperor. His coins carry Claudius's portrait.

people.name: Helena of Adiabene
people.summary: Queen of the Parthian vassal kingdom of Adiabene who converted to Judaism with her son Izates, moved to Jerusalem, relieved the famine of c. 46-48 and was buried in the monumental "Tomb of the Kings".
people.detail: Rabbinic sources remember her golden lamp over the Temple entrance and her Nazirite vows. Pausanias admired her tomb's mechanical door.
people.death: natural causes in Adiabene, c. 56; buried in Jerusalem

people.name: Antonius Felix
people.summary: Freedman brother of Pallas who governed Judaea c. 52-59, married three queens (including Drusilla, sister of Agrippa II), crushed bandits and the "Egyptian" prophet, and held Paul prisoner hoping for a bribe.
people.detail: Tacitus says he "exercised royal power with the mind of a slave". The sicarii first appeared under him, assassinating the former High Priest Jonathan.

people.name: Porcius Festus
people.summary: Procurator of Judaea c. 59-62 who heard Paul's appeal to Caesar and sent him to Rome after consulting Agrippa II; he died in office, and the interregnum allowed the stoning of James.
people.detail: Josephus describes his campaigns against sicarii and a dispute over a wall built by the priests to block Agrippa's view of the Temple.

people.name: Venutius
people.summary: Brigantian noble, former husband of Queen Cartimandua and once loyal to Rome, who led the anti-Roman faction against her in the 50s and overthrew her in 69; the war against him was taken up by Petillius Cerialis from 71.
people.detail: Tacitus calls him second only to Caratacus in military skill. His end is unknown.

people.name: Clodius Macer

roles.t: Legate of the legion in Africa

people.summary: Legate of III Augusta who rebelled against Nero in 68, raised a new legion and cut Rome's African grain supply, striking coins in the name of the Senate without claiming the title of emperor; Galba had him killed.
people.detail: His denarii, with legends such as L CLODI MACRI and a portrait of Libertas, are prized rarities.

people.name: Yohanan ben Zakkai

roles.t: Head of the court at Yavneh

people.summary: Pharisaic sage whom rabbinic tradition credits with escaping besieged Jerusalem and founding the academy at Yavneh, laying the foundations of rabbinic Judaism after the Temple's destruction.
people.detail: He issued ordinances (taqqanot) adapting Temple rituals such as the shofar on the Sabbath and the lulav to synagogue practice. His pupils included Eliezer ben Hyrcanus and Joshua ben Hananiah.

people.name: Columella
people.summary: Agronomist from Gades who wrote twelve books On Agriculture and a shorter On Trees, the most complete Roman account of estate farming, including a famous calculation of vineyard profits.
people.detail: He owned estates near Rome at Ardea, Carseoli and Alba, and served as a military tribune in Syria (inscription from Tarentum).

people.name: Hero of Alexandria
people.summary: Mathematician and engineer of the mid first century AD whose works on pneumatics, automata, mechanics, surveying and artillery describe the aeolipile steam turbine, programmable automata and the formula for the area of a triangle from its sides.
people.detail: His date rests on the lunar eclipse of 62 AD in the Dioptra. He probably taught at the Museum of Alexandria.
